subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Ocean Worlds
description: Learn Ocean Worlds in one minute.

hook.text: Some exoplanets may be covered entirely by deep global oceans—water worlds with no land at all.

buildup.text: If a planet has enough water and the right temperature, oceans could be hundreds of kilometers deep.

discovery.text: K2-18b showed water vapor in its atmosphere in 2019. It may be a 'Hycean' world—a hydrogen-rich ocean planet.

twist.text: Deep enough oceans create exotic high-pressure ice at the bottom—not from cold, but from extreme pressure alone.

climax.text: JWST detected possible signs of dimethyl sulfide on K2-18b—a molecule made by life on Earth. The debate rages on.

punchline.text: Worlds of endless ocean. One might even carry a chemical hint of life.

quiz.question: What makes K2-18b a significant exoplanet discovery?
options: JWST detected possible biosignature molecules in its atmosphere
It is the closest ocean world to our solar system
It has a visible ocean surface photographed by telescopes

details.summary: Ocean worlds are exoplanets potentially covered entirely by deep liquid water oceans, possibly hundreds of kilometers deep with no exposed land. Some may have water trapped under thick ice shells or hydrogen atmospheres.
details.whyItMatters: If ocean worlds are habitable, the number of potentially life-bearing planets increases dramatically. They challenge the assumption that land and plate tectonics are necessary for biology.
takeaways: Planets potentially covered entirely by deep liquid water
Could be common based on exoplanet density measurements
Challenge traditional habitability assumptions about land

faq.question: Would an ocean world be habitable?
faq.answer: Possibly, but with challenges. Without exposed rock, chemical weathering and the carbonate-silicate cycle that stabilizes Earth's climate would be absent. Very deep oceans would have high-pressure ice at the bottom, isolating the ocean from the rocky interior.

faq.question: How do we identify ocean worlds?
faq.answer: By measuring both size (transit method) and mass (radial velocity), astronomers calculate density. Planets with densities between pure rock and pure water suggest significant water content. Atmospheric spectroscopy via JWST could detect water-rich atmospheres consistent with ocean surfaces below.
